topic.subject: science
topic.title: Solutions, solubility and concentration
topic.scope: Solute, solvent, saturated and unsaturated solutions, effect of temperature on solubility, mass percent concentration, dissolving vs melting, why stirring only speeds dissolving, suspension vs colloid vs solution

nodes.name: Components of a solution
external_prereqs: difference between a pure substance and a mixture

nodes.name: Solute and solvent
Solute is what dissolves; solvent is what it dissolves in (usually the larger part)
Water is a common solvent but not the only one
A solution is homogeneous; particles stay mixed and invisible
Dissolving versus melting
Dissolving: solute particles spread between solvent particles, both stay the same substances
Melting: a single pure solid turns to liquid on heating
Total mass is conserved when a solute dissolves
Solubility and saturation
Saturated and unsaturated solutions
A saturated solution cannot dissolve more of that solute at that temperature
Undissolved solid at the bottom means the liquid above is saturated
Factors affecting solubility and dissolving
Solubility of most solids rises with temperature
Stirring only speeds up dissolving; it does not change how much can dissolve
Solubility of gases in water falls as temperature rises
Solubility differs from substance to substance
Concentration of a solution
Mass percent concentration
Mass percent = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100
Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent
Concentration does not depend on how much solution is taken
external_prereqs: ratio stays same when both quantities scale

nodes.name: Solutions, suspensions and colloids
Telling the three mixtures apart
Suspension: large particles settle on standing, are filterable and scatter light
Colloid: particles do not settle, pass through filter paper, scatter light (Tyndall effect)
True solution: particles tiny, do not settle, not filterable, do not scatter light

misconceptions.statement: The solute is the substance present in the larger amount.
misconceptions.why: Students link the bigger quantity with the main or important part, and so with the solute.
misconceptions.fix: The solute is the substance that dissolves and the solvent is the substance that dissolves it. The solvent is usually the larger part, as water is in sugar water.

probe.question: 10 g of sugar is dissolved in 90 g of water. Which one is the solute?
probe.wrong_answer: Water, because there is more of it.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more important

misconceptions.statement: Only water can act as a solvent.
misconceptions.why: Water is the only solvent students meet in daily life and in school experiments.
misconceptions.fix: Many liquids are solvents. Petrol dissolves grease and nail polish remover dissolves nail polish. Water is called the universal solvent only because it dissolves many substances.

probe.question: What can be used to remove a grease stain from cloth when water fails?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing else dissolves grease, because only water is a solvent.

misconceptions.root_belief: the one familiar example is the whole category

misconceptions.statement: If a solution is left undisturbed for a long time, the dissolved particles slowly sink to the bottom.
misconceptions.why: Students expect anything heavier than water to sink, as mud does.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolved particles are tiny and spread evenly through the solvent. They stay mixed and do not settle however long the solution stands.

probe.question: A salt solution is kept in a jar for a month. Where is the salt?
probe.wrong_answer: It has settled at the bottom of the jar.

misconceptions.root_belief: heavier things always sink
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about dissolving and particle models (e.g. Driver-type research)

misconceptions.statement: Sugar dissolves in water because the sugar melts.
misconceptions.why: Both processes make the solid seem to vanish into a liquid, so students use one word for both.
misconceptions.fix: Melting is a solid turning to liquid by heating. In dissolving, solid particles spread out between water particles with no heating and the sugar is still sugar.

probe.question: Why does sugar disappear when stirred into cold water?
probe.wrong_answer: The sugar melts in the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: outcomes that look alike have the same cause
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom research on dissolving and melting confusion in school students

misconceptions.statement: When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar turns into water.
misconceptions.why: Students see only a clear liquid afterwards and think the solid changed its identity.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolved sugar is still sugar, just broken into tiny particles mixed among the water particles. Evaporating the water brings the sugar back.

probe.question: A sugar solution is boiled until the water is gone. What is left?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because the sugar had turned into water.

misconceptions.root_belief: substances change identity when mixed together
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas on dissolving and conservation of substance

misconceptions.statement: When sugar dissolves in water, it disappears, so the solution weighs less than water plus sugar.
misconceptions.why: What cannot be seen is assumed to have gone, so it is assumed to have no mass.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolved sugar is still there and still has mass. The mass of the solution equals the mass of water plus the mass of sugar.

probe.question: 100 g water and 10 g sugar are mixed and the sugar dissolves. What is the mass of the solution?
probe.wrong_answer: 100 g, because the sugar has disappeared.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: conservation-of-matter studies on dissolving (Piagetian and later science education research)

misconceptions.statement: Stirring makes more sugar dissolve than would dissolve without stirring.
misconceptions.why: Students think more effort gives a bigger result, and stirred drinks seem sweeter sooner.
misconceptions.fix: Stirring only helps the solute dissolve faster. The maximum amount that can dissolve at a given temperature is the same.

probe.question: A saturated sugar solution is stirred hard for 10 minutes. Can more sugar now dissolve?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, stirring makes room for more sugar.

misconceptions.root_belief: more effort means more result
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students confusing rate of dissolving with extent of dissolving

misconceptions.statement: Without stirring, sugar will never dissolve in water.
misconceptions.why: Students see stirring done every time and treat it as essential.
misconceptions.fix: Sugar dissolves by itself as particles slowly spread out. Stirring only brings fresh water to the solid and speeds this up.

probe.question: A sugar cube is left in still water for a day. Will it dissolve?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it needs stirring to dissolve.

misconceptions.root_belief: nothing happens unless something pushes it

misconceptions.statement: A saturated solution cannot dissolve any substance at all, even a different one.
misconceptions.why: Students read saturated as completely full and ignore that the limit is for one solute.
misconceptions.fix: Saturated means no more of that same solute can dissolve at that temperature. Another solute, such as salt in a sugar solution, can still dissolve.

probe.question: A saturated sugar solution can take no more sugar. Can a pinch of salt dissolve in it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the solution is full and nothing more can dissolve.

misconceptions.root_belief: one limit applies to everything

misconceptions.statement: If solid lies undissolved at the bottom, the liquid above it contains no dissolved solute.
misconceptions.why: Students look at the visible solid and cannot see dissolved solute in the clear liquid.
misconceptions.fix: If solid stays undissolved, the liquid above is already saturated. It is full of dissolved solute and cannot take any more.

probe.question: Extra sugar lies at the bottom of a beaker of water. How much sugar is in the clear liquid above?
probe.wrong_answer: None, all the sugar is at the bottom.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas on saturated solutions and the solid-solution equilibrium

misconceptions.statement: Heating water does not change how much solid it can dissolve, it only makes dissolving quicker.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the rate of dissolving with the amount that can dissolve.
misconceptions.fix: For most solids, more solute dissolves in hot water than in cold water. Heating raises solubility, not just the speed.

probe.question: A saturated solution at 30 degrees C is heated to 60 degrees C. Can more potassium nitrate dissolve?
probe.wrong_answer: No, heating only makes it dissolve faster.

misconceptions.root_belief: conditions change only speed, never the limit
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about temperature and solubility

misconceptions.statement: Gases dissolve more in warm water, as solids do.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the solid rule that hot water dissolves more.
misconceptions.fix: Gases are less soluble in warm water. That is why a warm soft drink loses its fizz and fish struggle in warm water.

probe.question: Does a pond hold more oxygen on a hot summer day or a cool day?
probe.wrong_answer: More on the hot day, as warm water dissolves more.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: At the same temperature, the same amount of water dissolves the same mass of any solid.
misconceptions.why: Students think of water as having a fixed capacity, whatever the solid.
misconceptions.fix: Each substance has its own solubility. At the same temperature, 100 g of water dissolves far more sugar than salt.

probe.question: 100 g of water dissolves about 36 g of salt at room temperature. How much sugar can it dissolve?
probe.wrong_answer: About 36 g as well.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a category behave alike

misconceptions.statement: Mass percent is the mass of solute divided by the mass of solvent, times 100.
misconceptions.why: Students find it natural to compare solute with the water it is put in.
misconceptions.fix: The mass of the whole solution, solute plus solvent, goes in the denominator. Mass percent = solute mass divided by solution mass, times 100.

probe.question: 20 g of salt is dissolved in 80 g of water. What is the mass percent of the solution?
probe.wrong_answer: 25 percent.

misconceptions.root_belief: a part is compared with the other part
misconceptions.source_hint: research on part-part versus part-whole ratio errors in percentage and concentration

misconceptions.statement: The mass of a solution is just the mass of the solvent used.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the solvent as the main material and the solute as a small addition.
misconceptions.fix: The solution contains both solvent and solute, so its mass is the sum of both.

probe.question: 5 g of sugar is dissolved in 95 g of water. What is the mass of the solution?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the main ingredient counts toward the total

misconceptions.statement: The concentration of a solution is just how much solute it contains, whatever the amount of solvent.
misconceptions.why: Students use one quantity, the solute mass, and ignore the ratio to the whole.
misconceptions.fix: Concentration compares solute with the whole solution. The same solute in more solvent gives a more dilute solution.

probe.question: 10 g of salt is dissolved in 100 g of water in beaker A and in 200 g of water in beaker B. Which is more concentrated?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are equally concentrated because both have 10 g of salt.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one quantity matters, ignore the ratio
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas of concentration versus amount

misconceptions.statement: A small spoonful taken from a bottle of salt solution is less concentrated than the whole bottle.
misconceptions.why: Students think a smaller quantity means a weaker effect.
misconceptions.fix: A solution is uniform, so any sample has the same concentration as the whole. Only the amount of solute in it is smaller.

probe.question: A bottle holds 10 percent salt solution. What is the concentration of one spoonful taken from it?
probe.wrong_answer: Less than 10 percent, as the spoonful is small.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on confusing concentration with amount of solution

misconceptions.statement: Muddy water is a solution because the mud mixes with the water.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, mixed in and dissolved are used as if they meant the same thing.
misconceptions.fix: Mud particles are large and settle on standing, so muddy water is a suspension. In a solution the particles are tiny and never settle.

probe.question: Muddy water is left standing for an hour and clear water appears above the mud. Is it a solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the mud had mixed in with the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: mixed together means dissolved
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's categories of mixing and dissolving

misconceptions.statement: If a mixture looks uniform and its particles cannot be seen, it must be a true solution, so milk is a solution.
misconceptions.why: Students judge by naked-eye look, so uniform means dissolved.
misconceptions.fix: Colloids such as milk look uniform but their particles are bigger than in a solution, and they scatter a beam of light. Looking uniform does not make it a solution.

probe.question: Milk looks the same everywhere and shows no visible particles. What type of mixture is it?
probe.wrong_answer: A solution, because no particles are visible.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: A colloid can be separated by ordinary filter paper, like a suspension.
misconceptions.why: Students think a filter removes anything that is not dissolved.
misconceptions.fix: Colloid particles are small enough to pass through ordinary filter paper. Only suspension particles are left behind.

probe.question: Will filter paper separate the milk fat from milk?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the fat stays on the filter paper.

misconceptions.root_belief: a filter removes everything not dissolved

misconceptions.statement: A beam of light is visible inside salt solution just as in a colloid.
misconceptions.why: Students think clear liquids behave alike, so a torch beam should show in any of them.
misconceptions.fix: Particles in a true solution are too small to scatter light, so the beam is not seen. Only colloids and suspensions scatter it.

probe.question: A torch beam is shone through salt water in a dark room. What will you see?
probe.wrong_answer: A bright path of light through the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: same appearance means same behaviour
